en: The Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of the Four Categories Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of Illuminating Teaching, Subject Faxian, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was staying alone in a quiet chamber, and this thought arose in his mind:
"Whatever fears, terrors, calamities, obstacles, diseases, or faults there may be among sentient beings in the world—
whether already arisen or yet to arise— all belong to the foolish;
for the wise, they do not exist."
After the Venerable Ānanda had reflected upon these matters, he rose from his seat and went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet; once his salutations were complete, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
While I was alone in a quiet room, this thought arose in my mind:
"All matters such as fear and alarm that exist in the world belong only to the foolish;
for the wise, they do not exist."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.”
Ānanda replied, “Indeed, World-Honored One!”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
Thus, all matters of fear and alarm in the world—whether already arisen or yet to arise, such as calamities, obstacles, illnesses, and transgressions—all belong to the foolish;
for the wise, they do not exist.
Ānanda! It is just as if someone were to pile up dry reeds and they were set ablaze; the fear and other such reactions of that foolish person would be exactly like this.
Ānanda! Thus, throughout the past, future, and present worlds, fools encounter calamities while the wise do not;
fools encounter obstacles and difficulties while the wise do not.
The foolish person has illness, while the wise person is without illness;
the foolish person has faults, while the wise person is without faults. Ānanda!

You should know that these are the qualities of fools and these are the qualities of the wise. Having understood those qualities of fools, one should distance oneself from them and practice the qualities of the wise.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
"You should train yourself thus.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by a 'foolish person'?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"A foolish person is one who is ignorant because they lack understanding."
The foolish people of the world do not understand the Dharma; therefore, they are called "fools.
What is it that they do not understand?

They do not understand that the objects of the Dharma consist of four categories: namely, they do not understand the Dharma of the elements (*dhātu*), they do not understand the Dharma of the sense bases (*āyatana*), they do not understand the Dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and they do not understand the Dharma of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
“Ānanda! Because one cannot fully comprehend such a Dharma as this, one is therefore called a fool. Ānanda said:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so. Those who do not understand these four dharmas are called fools.”
Furthermore, why is one called a wise person?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"One who is called a wise person is so named because they discern phenomena and thoroughly understand what is right and what is wrong."
What is thorough comprehension?

Thorough comprehension of the objects of phenomena also consists of four categories: namely, thorough comprehension of the phenomena of the elements (*dhātu*), thorough comprehension of the phenomena of the sense bases (*āyatana*), thorough comprehension of the phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and thorough comprehension of the phenomena of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
"One who is well able to understand such dharmas as these is therefore called a person of wisdom.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"One who thoroughly understands this dharma is called a wise person."
"And what realm of phenomena does this wise one understand?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You have asked well; I shall explain it for you."
Regarding what are called the elements (dhātu), there are many kinds, namely: the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element;
the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element;
the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; [and so forth].
The tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element;
the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element;
the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
Regarding these eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the wise person understands them as they truly are.

Furthermore, there are six elements, namely: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element. Regarding these six elements, the wise person understands them as they truly are.

"Furthermore, there are six elements, namely: the element of joy, the element of pleasure, the element of suffering, the element of equanimity, the element of affliction, and the element of ignorance. These six elements are understood by the wise as they truly are."

"Furthermore, there are six elements, namely: the element of sensual desire, the element of ill will, the element of non-ill will, the element of harmfulness, the element of non-harmfulness, and the element of renunciation. A wise person thoroughly understands these six elements as they truly are."

"Furthermore, there are four elements, namely the element of sensation, the element of perception, the element of mental formations, and the element of consciousness. A wise person thoroughly understands these four elements as they truly are."
"Furthermore, there are three realms, namely the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; regarding these three realms, the wise person understands them as they truly are."
“Furthermore, there are three realms, namely the lower realm, the middle realm, and the upper realm; regarding these three realms, the wise person understands them as they truly are.”

“Furthermore, there are three realms, namely: the wholesome realm, the unwholesome realm, and the indeterminate realm. Regarding these three realms, the wise person understands them as they truly are.”

“Furthermore, there are three realms, namely: the realm of those in training (śaikṣa), the realm of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and the realm of both those in training and those beyond training. A wise person thoroughly understands these three realms as they truly are.”

“Furthermore, there are two realms, namely the realm with outflows (sāsrava-dhātu) and the realm without outflows (anāsrava-dhātu). Regarding these two realms, the wise person understands them as they truly are.”
“Furthermore, there are two realms, namely the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm; these two realms, the wise person understands as they truly are.”
“Ānanda! Regarding such elements as these, those who possess wisdom are well able to comprehend them thoroughly.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Once that wise one has thus thoroughly understood the phenomena of the elements (dhātu), how does he further thoroughly understand the phenomena of the sense bases (āyatana)?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Regarding the 'bases of phenomena' (dharmāyatana), they refer to the twelve bases:
the eye-base, the form-base, the ear-base, the sound-base, the nose-base, the odor-base, the tongue-base, the taste-base, the body-base, the tangible-base, the mind-base, and the phenomenon-base."
"These twelve bases, those of wisdom understand as they truly are.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Once the wise have thus understood the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how do they further understand the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The wise should know that the twelvefold law of dependent origination arises from causes and conditions; because of causes and conditions, all phenomena (*dharma*) come to be.”

What are the causal conditions? They are as follows: conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; and conditioned by birth arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. Thus does this entire great mass of suffering arise.

If one thoroughly understands the aforementioned phenomena of dependent origination—that their causal nature is empty, such that they exist when conditions assemble and cease to exist when conditions disperse;
and since these conditional phenomena do not exist, all dharmas likewise do not exist.

That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease. Thus, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
"Such phenomena of arising and ceasing, the wise should understand as they truly are.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Once that wise person has understood, as it truly is, the phenomena of dependent origination, how then does he comprehend the principles of what is possible and what is impossible?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Regarding the principle of the impossible: it is impossible for one who has performed unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind to obtain a desirable and wholesome karmic retribution."
If one were to perform various wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, yet still receive unwholesome retribution, such a thing is impossible.
What is possible is this: that by performing various wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, one receives the desired, superior, and wondrous fruits of retribution; this is indeed possible.
"If one creates unwholesome karma through body, speech, and mind, and thereby obtains the corresponding unwholesome retribution, such a thing is indeed possible.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"

Regarding what is called "an impossibility": it refers to the performance of unwholesome karma through body, speech, and mind; that by such causes and conditions one might, after death, be reborn among humans or devas as a result superior to what was sought—that is impossible.
If one were to perform wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, yet fall into the evil destinies, such a thing is impossible.
What is possible is this: that by performing various wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, one is born among humans or devas; this is indeed possible.
"If one commits evil karma and falls into the evil realms, such a thing is possible.
Furthermore, Ānanda! It is impossible for two Buddhas to appear in the world simultaneously."
It is possible for one Buddha to appear in the world; however,
it is impossible for two wheel-turning monarchs (cakravartin) to appear in the world simultaneously—
it is only possible for one wheel-turning monarch to appear.

Thus, it is impossible for a woman to become a Wheel-Turning King who governs and transforms the world, or even to become a Lord of the Four Heavenly Kings, a Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, a Great Brahmā King, or to attain the unsurpassed enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha; such things cannot occur.

If there should be a man endowed with the marks of a great being, adorned with merit and wisdom, who becomes a wheel-turning monarch appearing in the world, and even goes on to attain unsurpassed enlightenment—this is indeed possible.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

It is impossible for one who possesses right view to commit the five heinous crimes—killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, or shedding the blood of a Buddha."
"It is possible that an ordinary, foolish worldling with wrong views might commit the five heinous crimes.
Furthermore, Ānanda, it may happen that a person of right view who has received the full precepts, having himself broken those precepts, comes to slander his ācārya, saying: "

"This ācārya is not skilled in the dharmas of the precepts, nor is he able to receive and uphold the prohibitive rules; I shall select another ācārya to receive instruction in the dharmas of the precepts."

Having spoken these words, he went to other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to select a teacher from among them; or, having seen certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas engaged in various frivolous disputations, he approached them.
For one who lacks ethical discipline, it is impossible to rely on such a person as an acharya and seek tranquility and liberation from the three realms of existence.
However, if one acts with such foolishness and wrong views as to seek [ordination] under them, that is indeed possible.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a person does not sever the root afflictions and the secondary afflictions, then because of those afflictions, they diminish their roots of goodness, obstruct wisdom, and shroud the true, tranquil dharma of nirvāṇa."
It is impossible for that person to fully comprehend the four foundations of mindfulness.

However, it is possible for one who has severed the root afflictions and secondary afflictions, who is well able to understand the Dharma of the four foundations of mindfulness, and who seeks to proceed toward Nirvana.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is impossible for a person who does not sever the afflictions to thoroughly understand the four foundations of mindfulness, realize the seven factors of awakening, and proceed toward Nirvāṇa."
If a person, having severed the defilements, realizes the four foundations of mindfulness, attains the seven factors of enlightenment, and proceeds toward Nirvana, such a thing is possible.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a person does not sever the afflictions, yet claims to comprehend the four foundations of mindfulness, realize the seven factors of awakening, reach the end of suffering, proceed toward nirvāṇa, attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or even achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening—such a thing is impossible."

If one were to sever the afflictions, fully comprehend the four foundations of mindfulness, realize the seven factors of enlightenment, reach the end of suffering, proceed toward Nirvana, attain the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha, or even achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—such a thing is possible.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The wise person, in this manner, realizes and penetrates the dharma of what is possible and what is impossible as it truly is.
You all should train yourselves accordingly.”
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having heard such an unprecedented teaching, I have attained the flavor of the Deathless and am deeply filled with joy and gladness.”
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named, and how should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This sutra is named 'The Dharma Gate of the Four Categories,' and it is also named 'The Mirror of Dharma,' and it is also named 'The Drum of Ambrosia,' and it is also named 'The Many Realms. You should receive and uphold these names."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of Four Chapters Spoken by the Buddha.
